definitions.explanation: The fifth basic taste alongside sweet, sour, salty, and bitter. A pleasant savory taste found in foods containing glutamates and nucleotides, such as aged cheese, fermented products, and meat.
More generally, the pleasing flavor or richness of food that makes it delicious.

examples.japanese: {昆布|こんぶ}から{旨味|うまみ}が{出|で}る。
examples.english: Umami comes out of the kelp.

examples.japanese: {発酵食品|はっこうしょくひん}は{旨味|うまみ}が{豊|ゆた}かだ。
examples.english: Fermented foods are rich in umami.

examples.japanese: {旨味|うまみ}は{甘味|あまみ}・{酸味|さんみ}・{塩味|しおみ}・{苦味|にがみ}に{続|つづ}く{五番目|ごばんめ}の{味覚|みかく}だ。
examples.english: Umami is the fifth taste after sweet, sour, salty, and bitter.

examples.japanese: この{料理|りょうり}は{旨味|うまみ}がある。
{煮込|にこ}むと{旨味|うまみ}が{増|ま}す。
このスープは{素材|そざい}の{旨味|うまみ}が{凝縮|ぎょうしゅく}されていて{本当|ほんとう}においしい。
examples.english: This soup has concentrated flavor from the ingredients and is really delicious.

notes:
ORTHOGRAPHY:
Can also be written as {旨み|うまみ} or うま{味|み}. The kanji {旨|うま} means "delicious" or "tasty."

SCIENTIFIC BACKGROUND:
Umami was identified by Japanese chemist {池田菊苗|いけだきくなえ} in 1908, who discovered that glutamate was responsible for the savory taste of {昆布|こんぶ} (kelp). The term "umami" is now used internationally in food science.

UMAMI-RICH FOODS:
・{昆布|こんぶ} - kelp
・{鰹節|かつおぶし} - dried bonito flakes
・{味噌|みそ} - miso
・{醤油|しょうゆ} - soy sauce
・{椎茸|しいたけ} - shiitake mushrooms
・チーズ - cheese (especially aged)
・トマト - tomatoes

COLLOCATIONS:
・{旨味|うまみ}を{引|ひ}き{出|だ}す - to bring out the umami
・{旨味|うまみ}が{染|し}み{込|こ}む - for umami to soak in
・{旨味成分|うまみせいぶん} - umami compounds
